title: Cost economics discovery - Redwood & Lyric Capital
summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics, batching/caching levers, and whether Lyric should start on hosted or move to Dedicated/Private for cost predictability and data controls. Customer wants a pilot + benchmark to validate per-token cost at 1000 qps bursts and monthly budget constraints.
next_steps: Jordan to send model-level per-token pricing deck and sample cost spreadsheet (including batching scenarios)
Maya to provision benchmark config and run sample workload with Lyric prompts next week
Lyric to share sample workload and SLOs (latency targets, qps forecast)
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark and pilot terms - week of 2026-03-16
action_items: Jordan Patel: Send pricing deck + per-token cost spreadsheet - due 2026-03-09
Maya Chen: Prepare benchmark config, include batching/caching toggles - due 2026-03-10

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07 15:30 PST
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Samir (Lyric Head of ML), Hannah (Infra), Daniel (CPO)

Summary: quick cost econ discovery on hosted vs dedicated/private, want to understand per-token math, batching savings, caching.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching, kv cache, budget, dedicated capacity, SOC2/KMS/VPC.

[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, excited to chat through cost econ and where redwood fits, um feel free to interrupt.
[00:00:06] Samir: yeah thanks, Jordan, quick context - we run inference for quant research and a trading insights product, about 200 engineers, peaks up to 1k qps for short prompts, average prompt length ~120 tokens, responses ~180 tokens. Our budget is tight - looking to keep monthly inference spend under $30k to start.
[00:00:28] Maya: great, that helps. are those 1k qps sustained or burst?
[00:00:32] Samir: mostly bursts, like spikes for earnings calls and bulk reranks. sustained baseline is closer to 120 qps.
[00:00:40] Hannah: security side - we need SOC2, audit logs, and KMS integration. we're exploring VPC/private too.
[00:00:47] Jordan: totally. so two parallel questions: unit economics and deployment mode. on unit econ we break down per-token cost by model variant and effective batching/cache hit rate; on deployment we can recommend starting hosted to validate, then move to Dedicated or Private if predictability/security needs outweigh the friction.
[00:01:02] Daniel: what's the delta between hosted and dedicated usually? like per-token we care about.
[00:01:07] Maya: it depends on utilization and batching. hosted is usage-based per-token. dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and a lower per-token unit cost at higher commit levels - but you pay for reserved capacity whether you use it or not. For example, for a 24/7 8-GPU pool at commit we often see effective per-token cost drop ~20-45% for heavy workloads because you amortize infra and can run more efficient batching.
[00:01:29] Samir: okay, but our pattern is bursty - would dedicated still make sense?
[00:01:33] Maya: maybe - we have burst policies and autoscale/burst credit for Dedicated to handle spikes. the economics depend on how much of the month you actually use the reserved GPUs. if bursts are short and unpredictable, hosted + caching/better batching may be cheaper initially.
[00:01:49] Jordan: one lever that helps both modes is prefix/KV caching - if you have repeated prefixes or rerank contexts we can cache KV states and dramatically reduce per-token compute for subsequent calls. what's your hit rate on repeated contexts?
[00:02:01] Samir: reranks hit a lot of reuse, maybe 30-40% reuse across requests, but the trading alert generation is more unique.
[00:02:09] Maya: perfect place for caching. in our models, a cache hit can reduce compute cost of the remainder of seq by up to 60-80% depending on where the hit occurs. blockers are stateful routing and you need affinity for cache locality.
[00:02:24] Hannah: is that available in hosted? any security concerns with caching?
[00:02:29] Jordan: yes, hosted supports KV/prefix caching and we offer options for encrypting caches at rest with customer-managed keys in Dedicated/Private. shared hosted cache is multi-tenant but encrypted; if you need stricter controls we recommend Dedicated or Private where you can isolate or bring your own KMS.
[00:02:46] Daniel: can you quantify how batching changes price? like if we batch to 8 vs 1 what's the delta per token?
[00:02:52] Maya: rough numbers - batching improves hardware utilization. for transformer forward/backwards it's mostly forward path at inference; batching from 1 to 8 can save you 20-40% on GPU time per token depending on model and sequence length; larger batches more savings but latency increases.
[00:03:08] Samir: latency is a big SLO for us - under 200ms p95 for our interactive tool. how does batching affect p95?
[00:03:15] Maya: we tune batching with dynamic thresholds - we do small immediate dispatch and wait short micro-batch windows (e.g., 10-30ms) to accrue some batch. that usually keeps p95 within SLOs for <200ms requirements for short sequences. for strict real-time we can pin to smaller batches or even low-latency dedicated tails.
[00:03:30] Hannah: and quantization - we saw notes about 4-bit quant models. what are the quality / perf tradeoffs?
[00:03:35] Maya: quantization (4-bit/8-bit) reduces memory and can increase throughput; quality delta depends on model and evals - for some LLaMA-derivatives it's negligible for many tasks; for sensitive generation or high-precision tasks you want to run evals. we recommend a small quality evaluation set (we can run with your prompts) before switching.
[00:03:52] Daniel: sounds good. can you provide a worked example - say our 120 token input, 180 token output, at 1k bursts and baseline 120 qps?
[00:03:59] Jordan: sure. we'll send a simple spreadsheet but quick back-of-envelope - hosted per-token list price for a mid-sized open model might be X cents per 1k tokens, with our public rates we can show the per-req cost: 300 tokens -> multiply by per-token. then apply batching and an assumed cache hit (e.g., 30%) to show reductions. dedicated shifts to a fixed monthly commit and lowers marginal per-token. we'll send concrete numbers.
[00:04:26] Samir: can you do an example where we assume 30% cache, batching avg 4, and quantized variant? what's the relative reduction?
[00:04:33] Maya: sure - with those assumptions you'd see roughly 40-60% effective reduction vs naive unbatched hosted with no cache and fp16 model. exacts matter - we'll put scenarios.
[00:04:44] Hannah: security again - SOC2 yes, and we need SAML SSO and audit logs for model access. also data residency - EU region for some customers.
[00:04:54] Jordan: we support SOC2, SAML, RBAC, audit logs; region pinning and Private deployments let you keep everything in customer VPC. for KMS you can bring keys in Dedicated/Private and have encryption in transit and at rest.
[00:05:06] Samir: what about offline/on-prem - is that full feature parity?
[00:05:10] Maya: on-prem parity is close but some managed features (like global analytics and hosted billing) require control-plane connectivity. we offer air-gapped options for regulated customers but that adds setup time.
[00:05:20] Daniel: what's the onboarding timeline for a pilot?
[00:05:22] Jordan: for hosted pilot it's immediate - we can give API keys and run. for Dedicated pilot with reserved GPUs it's typically 4-8 weeks to provision depending on region and commit. Private/VPC or on-prem is 6-12+ weeks typically.
[00:05:35] Hannah: benchmark - we want Redwood to run our sample workload and show per-token cost at our mix. can you do that?
[00:05:40] Maya: yes absolutely. Maya: we'll need sample prompts, expected concurrency profile, and success criteria (e.g., p95 latency under 200ms, cost under $X/month). We'll run hosted and, if you'd like, a simulated Dedicated run using our cost model.
[00:05:54] Jordan: action items - we'll send pricing sheet + a few scenario runs. can we tentatively schedule follow-up on Mon 2026-03-16?
[00:06:00] Samir: Monday works.
[00:06:02] Daniel: yeah Monday is fine.
[00:06:05] Hannah: I'll upload the prompts and concurrency forecasts to the shared folder after this call.
[00:06:09] Jordan: perfect. thanks everyone. finishing notes: we'll include models, quant variants, expected savings from batching and cache, and a recommended path (hosted -> pilot -> dedicated if math works).
[00:06:21] Maya: and we'll include some knobs - batch window, batch size, cache TTLs, and autoscale/burst credit details so you can see where tradeoffs live.
[00:06:30] Samir: great, thanks.
[00:06:33] Jordan: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
